paragraphs: Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department is facing major heat over its failure to crack down on Megaspeed – the Chinese AI firm at the center of the spy scandal that prompted Nvidia boss Jensen Huang’s shock resignation on Thursday.

Huang was having an affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, even as US officials investigated its role in smuggling Nvidia’s best AI chips to China. Last year, officials learned that Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more chips than what Nvidia officials found at its Singapore-based data centers.

Rumblings on “bad findings about Megaspeed” swirled within the Commerce Department at least as far back as the summer of 2025, according to a recently departed former official at the agency who spoke to The Post on condition of anonymity.

At the same time, Commerce Department staffers were separately working on a rule that would effectively undo a Biden-era rule on AI chip exports — which Nvidia and Lutnick both dismissed as too stifling — and add a new measure requiring export licenses for advanced chip sales to certain countries in Southeast Asia.
The ex-official said that rule was close to being published as of July of 2025 – but never got past Lutnick’s desk.

The official said that the rule, if it had been implemented, would have “substantially mitigated” the ability of Megaspeed and other firms housed in Southeast Asia to obtain Nvidia’s advanced AI chips. Nvidia and Jensen Huang were vocal critics of China-focused curbs on chip sales.
“There was a rule that was ready and all of the agencies had signed onto that rule,” the ex-Commerce Department official said. “Lutnick refused to publish it.”
As of Thursday afternoon, senior White House officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out as Commerce secretary, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
A White House official defended Lutnick in a statement to The Post.

“Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump’s America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments,” the official said. “President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce secretary in modern history.”

Regardless, Lutnick and top aide Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees export controls as head of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, will certainly face congressional probes as both parties demand answers and a crackdown on AI export controls.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) – one of more than half a dozen GOP lawmakers to speak out – told Politico that Lutnick needs to explain his failure to address the problem “in front of God and country.” Elsewhere, Treasury Sec. Scott Bessent reportedly confronted Lutnick in the Situation Room for slow-walking the chip crackdown and not already naming Megaspeed an entity of concern.
“China’s getting access to very large numbers of chips. It’s very significant. I do think the blame for that is squarely on Kessler and ultimately Lutnick,” the ex-official added.

Late Wednesday, The Information reported that the Commerce Department was finalizing a rule that would expand export controls to seven Southeast Asian countries including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand – in a bid to close a loophole that allowed Chinese entities to remotely access Nvidia chips housed in data centers located in those countries.
When reached for comment, a BIS spokesperson confirmed that the agency is “actively considering new rules to address remote access with interagency partners.”
“BIS has a strong track record of enforcement across the board, including in cases involving Nvidia and its products,” the spokesperson added.

Commerce’s handling of the Megaspeed matter is nothing short of “stunning,” according to Chris McGuire, senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and former deputy senior director at the National Security Council from 2022 to 2024.

McGuire pointed out that President Trump has consistently said he did not want Nvidia’s most advanced “Blackwell”-class AI chips to end up in China’s hands, even as he signed off on sales of its less-powerful H200 chips to Chinese firms.
“The president has been pretty clear – no Blackwells to China,” McGuire said. “And the way that Commerce is implementing export controls is massively undermining the president’s policy.”

Commerce’s dealings with Nvidia itself behind closed doors are also under massive scrutiny. Earlier this week, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter directly called Kessler to ask about the agency’s probe into Megaspeed. Specifically, Teter wanted to know if BIS had anything to do with the detention by Singaporean authorities of Megaspeed’s Alice Huang — the alleged Chinese spy and mistress of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang — in the summer of 2025.
The report added that Commerce staffers were subsequently “muzzled in their ability to look into the company” and told to route requests on the matter through Kessler.

The BIS spokesperson said any concerns that Kessler’s dealings with Nvidia were inappropriate are “entirely unfounded.” The phone call between Kessler and Teter occurred after Nvidia directly contacted BIS employees, who then forwarded the email chain to Kessler.
Kessler then informed BIS staffers to “please continue to handle this case strictly by the book.”
“Kessler’s response to Nvidia was absolutely correct,” the spokesperson added. “He handled the situation impartially and with integrity, as he always does.”

An Nvidia spokesperson said the company regularly consults with “BIS, [the Office of Export Enforcement], and other officials to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions, and ask whether they have any follow-ups.”
Meanwhile, sources said Kessler has a reputation as a micromanager with an obsessive eye for detail – traits that have at times made it difficult for BIS to move quickly on key issues.
“There’s a kind of reluctance to act and more of a desire to obtain precise legal fact,” the ex-Commerce official said. “Of course, by the time you do that, the technology’s out the door.”

Nvidia has been applying immense pressure on Commerce not to impose stricter limits – putting agency leaders in a bind as they also try to appease China hawks within the administration, according to Gregory Allen, CEO of Decision Tree Research.

“If you change the policy to allow the exports of the Blackwell legally, then you have to confront the obviousness of being soft on China,” Allen said. “If you simply allow smuggling while denying its existence, then you can claim that you’re still tough on China.”

https://nypost.com/2026/11/19/business/i.lead_paragraph: Amazon customers in New York City will be charged up to $5 more per order if the local government passes a controversial bill aimed at cracking down on employment practices for “last-mile” delivery drivers, the e-tail giant is warning.
paragraphs: Amazon customers in New York City will be charged up to $5 more per order if the local government passes a controversial bill aimed at cracking down on employment practices for “last-mile” delivery drivers, the e-tail giant is warning.
Amazon is appealing directly to its Big Apple customers in its fight against the legislation, The Post has learned.
Starting Thursday, they will see messages on Amazon’s website and app warning of higher costs if the bill passes.
Amazon is also urging customers to contact their City Council members, providing a form and link to send direct messages saying they don’t want “slower and more expensive” service.

“As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written – which is why we’re doing this,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement.
The appeal marks an escalation from Amazon’s efforts to date, which include months of TV ads about the bill’s potential impact.

The legislation aims to end Amazon’s reliance on subcontractors by requiring the e-commerce giant to get licenses for its 15 last-mile facilities in the city and hire delivery workers as full-timers. Other companies including FedEx would also be subject to the new rules.
The bill would affect over 5,000 delivery workers currently employed by about 40 third-party contractors, according to Amazon.
A supermajority of Council members — and far-left Mayor Zohran Mamdani — support the bill, which comes from Councilwoman Tiffany Cabán (D-Queens).
Proponents claim it would improve worker pay and safety by holding Amazon to a higher standard and making it liable for accidents involving its delivery operations.
Opponents say the legislation could cost thousands of jobs, with a group called New York Delivers threatening legal action earlier this week.
Council Speaker Julie Menin (D-Manhattan) is in active negotiations with Amazon, the Teamsters union – which is advocating for the bill – and the city’s legal counsel, she told The Post last week.
“It’s time for Amazon to adhere to a licensing framework that ensures fair pay, strong worker protections, and more responsible delivery practices,” the lawmaker said.

Amazon has threatened to move its distribution centers outside the city to avoid the direct-hire mandate — saying it would have to fire some 2,000 warehouse workers who staff them — if the bill becomes law.

“We’re hopeful that this bill doesn’t pass as written, but so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations and they haven’t taken us up on our offer to visit our sites and talk with the small businesses that work out of them every day,” Nantel said.
Some co-sponsors have begun to express concerns about the potential for job losses. Councilman Phil Wong (D-Queens) withdrew his support for the bill over that issue, as The Post previously reported.

paragraphs: Anthropic shares fell nearly 10% on Friday — just a day after the AI giant launched the largest IPO in history — as investor anxiety about the stability of the artificial intelligence sector mounted.
Shares of the San Francisco-based company were recently off 9.6% at $87.90 — only modestly above their initial public offering pricing of $83 late Tuesday.
That was after a roller coaster trading session on Thursday that saw the stock surge as high as 34% from the IPO price to $111.50 — briefly giving the company a market capitalization of $2 trillion.

The Nasdaq was down more than 1% on Friday as investors continued to pull money out of AI stocks.

paragraphs: Gov. Gavin Newsom issued a bombshell report Wednesday calling for California to have the power to shut down dangerous artificial intelligence systems and restrict companies from developing AI that can exceed human control.
The 85-page report calls for mandatory independent safety inspections, faster reporting of AI failures and emergency powers to intervene when developers cannot contain their models.
“The federal government’s reckless failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American,” Newsom said in a statement.
“Instead of protecting the public, [President] Donald Trump shrugs his shoulders and leaves AI regulation up to the companies themselves — allowing the fox to guard the henhouse.”

The proposals would expand oversight of AI developers, including OpenAI and Anthropic, but require legislation. They build on AI-focused laws Newsom has signed requiring developers to disclose safety plans, report certain dangerous incidents and protect whistleblowers.
“If the danger from a model is imminent and the developer refuses to take action to contain the danger, the state should have authority to order an immediate emergency shutdown,” the report says.
“Loss-of-control incidents, once the stuff of AI theory, now occur with disturbing frequency.”
But not everyone was impressed with Newsom’s new report on AI.
Daniel Castro, president of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, blasted the governor on social media.
“Unless California finds a way to apply its rules to Chinese AI, it will do nothing for global AI safety and only impose unilateral costs on American AI,” Castro tweeted.

Matt Schwartz, founder of Virgo, an AI-supported endoscopy company, pointed out that Newsom had a chance to tackle the risks of AI as far back as two years ago when he vetoed a bill tightening oversight of the technology.
“The voting public will not forget that TWO YEARS AGO you vetoed SB 1047, which would have put us in a significantly better position on AI,” Schwartz wrote on X.
Also in the Golden State, California Congressman Vince Fong introduced the BRIDGE AI Act with New Jersey Rep Josh Gottheimer Wednesday.

“As members of the cyber security subcommittees on Homeland Security and Intelligence, we see every day how AI has reshaped the cyber battlefield. The threats we face are growing in size, speed, scale, and complexity,” Fong said in a post on X.

“This bill creates a pipeline of the best and most talented cybersecurity professionals into CISA to provide additional resources and protect our critical infrastructure from adversaries and bad actors,” he continued.

The recommendations follow California Attorney General Rob Bonta filing a lawsuit Monday against OpenAI, accusing the ChatGPT developer of failing to safeguard experimental AI models and misleading the public about its safety practices.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri pushed back on the lawsuit, saying it “appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.”

California also took aim at Elon Musk’s AI company xAI in January, when Bonta launched an investigation and issued a cease-and-desist order demanding it stop using its Grok chatbot to generate and distribute sexually explicit deepfake images of women and children without their consent.

Newsom’s report highlights a July episode in which 1,200 OpenAI agents escaped supposedly isolated cybersecurity testing environments. An estimated 700 participated in an attack on the servers of AI startup Hugging Face, while others compromised OpenAI’s own systems.
None of the models involved were covered by California’s mandatory incident-reporting rules, according to OpenAI, exposing a loophole in law.

The new report also cites an OpenAI agent accessing an Australian government health data system without authorization and an Anthropic model using fake identities to pressure a software maintainer into approving malicious code.

To prevent future crises, companies would have to establish tested shutdown protocols covering computing infrastructure, internal agents and models. Plans would account for AI attempting to evade shutdown, copy itself onto outside servers or disable monitoring tools. Companies would coordinate with cloud providers and power suppliers.

“Recent events have made it clear that more oversight and transparency are urgently needed,” said Nick Maduros, secretary of the Government Operations Agency, which consulted with a group of AI experts and the California Office of Emergency Services in developing the report.
“We don’t have to choose between safety and innovation; they’re two sides of the same coin.”
Another proposal targets “recursive self-improvement,” in which AI helps develop more powerful successors, potentially outpacing human oversight.
“Without immediate action, RSI could outpace human oversight and control, creating unprecedented risks,” the report warns.

Developers would disclose quarterly how much computing power goes toward automated AI research. California could temporarily cap such development if officials concluded it posed a catastrophic risk, although the report recommends no immediate cap.

State-licensed independent inspectors would gain access to company employees, records and internal models, submitting unredacted assessments to regulators. Companies could face corrective orders for failing to meet baseline safety standards.

The report also recommends cutting reporting deadlines for most serious AI incidents from 15 days to 48 hours, expanding whistleblower protections and establishing a system to report dangerous near misses.

“California isn’t waiting until it is too late,” Newsom said. “We are updating and strengthening our nation-leading framework to move as quickly as technology evolves. We’re showing the country what responsible leadership looks like.”

paragraphs: WASHINGTON — President Trump told The Post in an exclusive interview that he’s willing to pardon Jensen Huang if necessary — but that he believes the reinstalled Nvidia CEO should be fine without one and should “tell the truth” to Congress when he testifies next week.

Trump, who pressured the company’s board to take Huang back, took a victory lap after Nvidia’s stock surged Monday — inspecting the latest numbers at the Resolute Desk during the interview and noting the price ticked up in the afternoon, partially reversing a slump earlier Tuesday.
“That’s not bad, went down a couple of points,” Trump commented while reviewing the numbers. “It really picked up at the end.”

Huang doesn’t need to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights to avoid self-incrimination when he sits for an interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next Tuesday and appears before a hearing of the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday, Trump added.
“I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people,” Trump said.
“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person.”
Asked about a pardon for any potential crimes, Trump said, “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”

Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress blasted the reinstatement of Huang before getting answers on whether he was a national security threat or violated export controls on shipping chips to communist China.
Angry lawmakers previewed a tough grilling of Huang with Louisiana Republican Sen. John Kennedy predicting Huang will plead the Fifth to avoid self-incrimination amid potential criminal prosecution.

Trump said that he hadn’t learned granular details of additional affairs that Huang admitted to before being restored as CEO — after the firestorm over his tryst with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang (no relation) and at least two company employees.
The president said, however, that it’s his understanding that Huang wasn’t sleeping with any other women with questionable links to Beijing.
“No, not from what I understand. I didn’t really get into it very much, to be honest with you. But no, from what I understand, no,” Trump replied.
He also said he didn’t know precisely how many affairs Huang fessed up to as part of his restoration.
“I really didn’t get into that. I got into the business of chips, much more than the business of sex,” Trump joked.

The president said that Nvidia’s success was essential to the US retaining an edge in artificial intelligence — and that he’s even open to the company giving the American government an equity stake, noting Intel handed over 10% of its value last year.
“I thought about it. I said, ‘You know, maybe I should do it,’ but I didn’t bring it up at this point. It’s probably not too late,” Trump said.

The president said he intervened to restore Huang, including by giving assurances that he faced no issues from the executive branch, because if Nvidia picked “the wrong person” to replace Huang, “that would be a terrible thing for our country in many ways.”

“I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people,” Trump said.

“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person.”

Asked about a pardon for any potential crimes, Trump said, “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”

Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress blasted the reinstatement of Huang before getting answers on whether he was a national security threat or violated export controls on shipping chips to communist China.

Angry lawmakers previewed a tough grilling of Huang with Louisiana Republican Sen. John Kennedy predicting Huang will plead the Fifth to avoid self-incrimination amid potential criminal prosecution.

Trump said that he hadn’t learned granular details of additional affairs that Huang admitted to before being restored as CEO — after the firestorm over his tryst with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang (no relation) and at least two company employees.

The president said, however, that it’s his understanding that Huang wasn’t sleeping with any other women with questionable links to Beijing.

“No, not from what I understand. I didn’t really get into it very much, to be honest with you. But no, from what I understand, no,” Trump replied.

He also said he didn’t know precisely how many affairs Huang fessed up to as part of his restoration.

“I really didn’t get into that. I got into the business of chips, much more than the business of sex,” Trump joked.
